title: Test-time Multi-agent Coordination by Decomposed Value Gradient Flow

paper.title: Test-time Multi-agent Coordination by Decomposed Value Gradient Flow
paper.abstract: Abstract Offline multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) faces a persistent trade-off. Expressive generative policies can represent multi-modal coordination in the data, but cannot distinguish high-value regions, while value-optimized policies exploit the learned Q-function but collapse the multi-modal into a single dominant mode. A single agent’s mode collapse can break joint coordination, and simultaneous drift across agents can push the joint policy into unseen regions of the action space. We propose scalable coordination via optimal unified transport (SCOUT) , the first offline MARL framework to combine a generative foundation model with a learned value function through test-time action refinement. SCOUT trains two decoupled components: a flow-matching behavioral prior and a decomposed value function. At test-time, it transports behavioral samples toward high-value regions via Stein variational gradient descent. The number of transport steps controls adaptive test-time scaling, replacing a fixed regularization coefficient. Under the individual-global-max (IGM) principle, we prove a single-term KL bound on the joint soft-value gap that vanishes as transport converges, with an irreducible additive residual proportional to the IGM violation. Empirically, SCOUT achieves the best average performance across discrete and continuous offline MARL benchmarks and yields performance improvements in all offline-to-online configurations.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Offline MARL is motivated by the need to learn coordinated multi-agent behaviors in safety-critical or cost-constrained domains where active data collection is infeasible or expensive, e.g. , autonomous driving [ 1 ] , logistics [ 2 ] , and robotics [ 3 ] . In this setting, the learning objective is twofold. Agents must learn to coordinate their behavior from heterogeneous and suboptimal demonstrations, while avoiding the distributional shift that arises when the learned policy visits state-action regions unsupported by the data. Early offline MARL methods [ 4 , 5 , 6 ] rely on simple policy classes ( i.e. , Gaussian), which struggle to represent multi-modal and coordinated joint action distributions. When offline data contains a mixture of diverse coordination strategies, a unimodal policy often collapses onto a single mode and produces out-of-distribution joint actions that no agent in the data ever executed together. To address this expressiveness gap, recent works adopt powerful generative models, including diffusion models [ 7 , 8 ] and flow matching models [ 9 , 10 ] , as policy representations in offline MARL. Although these models improve the representational power of policy, their iterative sampling process incurs a high inference cost. MAC-Flow [ 10 ] and OM 2 P [ 9 ] mitigate this via one-step distillation and mean-flow generation, respectively. However, improved expressiveness and faster inference do not resolve a more fundamental limitation. Since the outcome policy is optimized against a learned Q-function, it inherently tends to collapse diverse coordination modes into a single or blurred one. Methods that parameterize a policy and optimize it to maximize a learned Q-function must balance value improvement against staying close to the behavioral distribution. A fixed regularization coefficient controls this trade-off. If it is too large, the policy stays too close to suboptimal data; if it is too small, the policy exploits errors in the learned Q-function and produces OOD actions. Although this tension is well-known in single-agent offline RL [ 11 , 12 ] , the multi-agent setting introduces the following compounding difficulty. Training-time value maximization deforms each agent’s policy away from the behavioral prior, and the regularization coefficient bounds how far each marginal may drift, but cannot bound the compound effect on the joint. Even when every marginal remains within its individual support, the joint policy can place mass on action combinations that no trajectory in the data ever visited ( i.e. , regions where the learned Q-function is least reliable). In fact, the data may support multiple distinct joint modes of comparably high estimated value, but committing each marginal to a single greedy mode at training time discards the others before the agent has any way to tell them apart. Once new interaction data arrives, the policy can no longer use it to discriminate which mode is truly higher-value, because the alternatives have already been suppressed. A natural alternative is to decouple two objectives, motivated by test-time training [ 13 , 14 , 15 ] . Instead of learning a policy that directly maximizes value, we keep the behavioral policy as a foundational prior and defer value-based refinement to test time. At deployment, we sample action candidates from this prior and then move them toward high-value regions using value gradients. The extent of this adjustment acts as adaptive control, replacing the need for a fixed regularization coefficient. In this work, we ask a question not yet studied by prior works: How do we avoid explicit policy parameterization for value maximization, and instead recover coordination at test time by directly transporting behavioral samples toward high-value regions? We answer this question with the proposed solution, SCOUT (scalable coordination via optimal unified transport) , an offline MARL framework that combines flow-matching behavioral priors with decomposed value gradient for test-time action refinement. Our key contributions are: • We propose a policy-free value maximization for offline MARL that separates behavioral modeling from value improvement, replacing training-time regularization tuning with a test-time refinement budget. • We derive decomposed value gradient transport under the IGM principle, enabling fully decentralized test-time refinement that recovers inter-agent coordination with a bounded approximation gap. • Empirically, test-time refinement strengthens coordination without retraining, achieving the best average performance in continuous and discrete domains. Notably, unlike existing flow-based MARL, our method yields improvements in all offline-to-online RL experiments.

sections.heading: 2 Related Works
sections.text: Offline MARL. Several works have explored the data-driven sequential decision-making problem, including offline RL and MARL, which aims to extract a return-maximizing policy within the support of an offline dataset. Specifically, offline MARL requires learning coordinated policies for multiple agents. This is not trivial because it requires modeling dependencies among agents in a combinatorially large joint action space. The simplest baselines are multi-agent extensions of single-agent offline RL methods, either by introducing conservatism in the value function [ 11 , 12 ] or the actor [ 16 ] , or by performing Bellman updates without querying out-of-distribution actions [ 17 ] . To further promote coordination, more advanced works are often combined with additional multi-agent design choices, such as value decomposition [ 5 , 18 ] , policy optimization with a centralized critic [ 4 , 6 ] , or a centralized world model [ 19 ] . However, these methods often struggle to capture the multi-modal distributions present in multi-agent offline datasets because of their limited policy expressiveness. To address this issue, recent work has adopted more expressive generative policies, including an autoregressive model [ 20 ] , diffusion models [ 7 ] , and flow matching [ 10 ] . However, these methods couple value learning with the generative process itself: they either anchor the policy via BC-like losses [ 21 , 22 , 10 , 23 ] , which produces overly conservative behavior, or backpropagate value gradients through iterative sampling [ 24 , 25 ] , which is unstable. In contrast, the proposed solution bypasses explicit policy parameterization altogether. Instead, Stein variational gradient [ 26 , 27 , 14 ] fields refine flow-generated action candidates toward high-value regions at test time. This enables adaptive test-time scaling while retaining generative expressiveness. Test-time action refinement. Our main idea in this work is based on test-time refinement ( i.e. , a ← a + ∇ a Q ​ ( s , a ) a\leftarrow a+\nabla_{a}Q(s,a) ) [ 13 ] , which refines actions from a base generative policy at inference time rather than during training. This paradigm has been explored along several directions in single-agent RL. Rejection sampling methods generate multiple action candidates and select the highest-valued one [ 28 , 29 ] . Gradient-based approaches directly optimize sampled actions via Q-function gradients [ 25 , 14 , 30 ] . Residual policies instead train a separate network to modify a base policy in noise or action space [ 31 , 32 ] . Complementary to these, optimal transport (OT) offers a principled framework for moving probability mass toward high-value regions [ 33 , 34 ] . More recently, particle-based methods adopt an OT viewpoint to transport samples toward value-preferred regions [ 35 ] . However, these approaches remain limited to single-agent settings. The proposed solution is motivated by this direction but specifically designed to solve the multi-agent coordination problem. This avoids explicit policy parameterization and naturally handles the combinatorial joint action space.

sections.heading: 4 Scalable Coordination via Optimal Unified Transport ( SCOUT )
sections.text: As motivated in Section 1 , our goal is to develop an offline MARL algorithm that can extract Q-maximizing multi-agent policies without explicit policy parameterization for value maximization. Following prior works [ 14 , 56 , 57 ] , we consider the MaxEnt surrogate of ( 2 ), 𝔼 a ∼ π [ Q ( s , a ) ] + α ℋ ( π ( ⋅ | s ) ) \mathbb{E}_{a\sim\pi}[Q(s,a)]+\alpha\mathcal{H}(\pi(\cdot|s)) , whose optimal policy takes the Boltzmann form π ∗ ​ ( a | s ) ∝ exp ⁡ ( Q ⁡ ( s , a ) / α ) \pi^{*}(a|s)\propto\exp(Q(s,a)/\alpha) . Rather than fitting an explicit actor to approximate π ∗ \pi^{*} , we construct a transport map that moves samples from μ \mu toward π ∗ \pi^{*} via variational gradient descent, using ∇ a Q \nabla_{a}Q as the driving force. Specifically, given a set of action candidates sampled from a flow-matching behavioral policy, we iteratively refine them at test time via the simplest possible update as a ← a + η ​ ∇ a Q ​ ( o , a ) a\leftarrow a+\eta\nabla_{a}Q(o,a) . The resulting refined actions constitute the implicit policy output, with the number of gradient steps L L serving as a tunable knob that controls coordination strength at deployment without retraining. Why do we need an implicit policy? This direction offers several appealing properties. First, because the initial actions are drawn from the behavioral policy, the implicit policy refines the behavioral prior rather than replacing it. Then, the transport budget provides an adaptive test-time scaling. When L = 0 L=0 , it recovers the best sampling from the behavioral policy, while increasing L L progressively pushes actions toward Q-maximizing regions. Furthermore, the gradient-based transport can discover actions beyond the reference distribution when the Q-function generalizes well.

sections.heading: 4.1 Why is this hard in multi-agent settings?
sections.text: The above idea and problem hold straightforwardly in the single-agent setting [ 14 , 48 ] , where the transport operates on a single action space 𝒜 \mathcal{A} guided by a single Q-function. However, extending this to multi-agent settings is non-trivial. Under the CTDE paradigm, each agent i i can only access its local observation o i o_{i} at test time. This means the action refinement must run independently for each agent, using only its local Q-function Q i ​ ( o i , a i ) Q_{i}(o_{i},a_{i}) and its own action particles. The refined joint action ( a 1 ∗ , … , a I ∗ ) (a_{1}^{*},\ldots,a_{I}^{*}) must be globally coherent. Namely, each agent’s refined action should be coordinated with those of other agents. This tension between decentralized execution and coordinated behavior has been a long-standing challenge in MARL [ 39 , 40 ] . The most common solution is the IGM principle [ 39 ] in ( 1 ), which ensures independent per-agent maximization to align with joint maximization. However, several practical questions remain. First, IGM guarantees alignment at the greedy argmax, but the gradient-based transport involves iterative updates that modify the particle distribution across multiple steps. It is unclear whether the per-agent transport dynamics remain aligned with the joint optimum throughout this process, especially when the critic must evaluate actions that are progressively shifted away from the behavioral support during training. Second, the individual behavioral prior might discard the inter-agent correlations present in the offline data. Even if the transport dynamics are correctly factorized, the initial particles may lack the coordination patterns necessary for effective joint behavior.

sections.heading: 4.4 Algorithm summary
sections.text: We summarize the SCOUT framework in Pseudocode 1 . Training alternates between two decoupled objectives: ( i ) the flow-matching loss ℒ BC \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{BC}} fits the individual behavioral prior with ODE in Pseudocode 2 , and the TD loss ℒ critic \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{critic}} learns decomposed Q functions whose targets are computed through the additive decomposition Q tot = ∑ i Q i Q_{\mathrm{tot}}=\sum_{i}Q_{i} using actions refined by L train L_{\mathrm{train}} transport steps in Pseudocode 3 . At test time, each agent independently generates P P behavioral candidates via ODE integration, refines them for L test L_{\mathrm{test}} steps of decomposed value gradient flow, and selects the highest- Q i Q_{i} particle. The transport budget ( L test , ϵ ) (L_{\mathrm{test}},\epsilon) need not match training. In particular, L test = 0 L_{\mathrm{test}}=0 recovers best-of- P P sampling, L test = L train L_{\mathrm{test}}=L_{\mathrm{train}} matches training conditions, and L test > L train L_{\mathrm{test}}>L_{\mathrm{train}} enables additional test-time scaling when the Q-function generalizes beyond the data support.

sections.heading: 4.5 Didactic example: Why do we need test-time value guidance, not training time?
sections.text: To illustrate the trade-off between training-time and test-time value incorporation, we design a two-agent coordination game (Figure 2 ( a )). Each agent selects a scalar action a i ∈ [ − 2 , 2 ] a_{i}\in[-2,2] , and the joint reward has two anti-correlated Gaussian modes: an optimal mode at ( − 1 , 1 ) (-1,1) with reward 4 4 and a sub-optimal mode at ( 1 , − 1 ) (1,-1) with reward 2 2 . The offline dataset consists of 400 transitions, with only 10 % 10\% near each peak. Both methods share the same VDN critic Q tot = Q 1 ​ ( a 1 ) + Q 2 ​ ( a 2 ) Q_{\mathrm{tot}}=Q_{1}(a_{1})+Q_{2}(a_{2}) . The key difference is how each method incorporates the Q-function. MAC-Flow jointly optimizes distillation and Q-maximization, forcing the projected one-step policy to balance behavioral cloning and value improvement during training. In this toy example, this training-time compromise anchors each agent’s output to the broad data distribution, while the decomposed Q-gradient alone cannot represent the anti-correlated structure, causing the policy to collapse near the origin (Figure 2 ( c )). In contrast, SCOUT keeps the behavioral flow unchanged and applies value guidance only at test time. This preserves the multi-modal prior, and five refinement steps are sufficient to move candidates toward the optimal mode (Figure 2 ( b )). In this setting, the selected per-agent actions align with the same anti-correlated mode because the additive utilities are trained from coordinated demonstrations. Figure 2: Toy example. sections.heading: 5.1 Experimental setup
sections.text: We evaluate SCOUT on two cooperative MARL testbeds with discrete and continuous action spaces, spanning 7 7 scenarios and 24 24 offline datasets. We first introduce the selected testbeds and baselines. SMACv1 . Agents control a team of units in StarCraft II micromanagement tasks against a built-in AI opponent. We test on four maps, including 3m , 8m , 2s3z , and 5m_vs_6m . Each map is paired with three offline dataset quality levels ( Good , Medium , Poor ) from the off-the-grid benchmark [ 58 ] , resulting in 12 12 configurations. The quality levels differ in the proportion of near-optimal trajectories, with Poor containing mostly suboptimal behavior. MA-MuJoCo. In this testbed, a single robot is factorized into multiple agents, with each agent responsible for a specific subset of the robot’s joints. This setup requires agents to learn coordinated behaviors to accomplish shared tasks. We source the corresponding offline datasets from [ 6 ] . Baseline. We organize baselines into three families by their policy type. For the Gaussian policy, BC , MATD3BC [ 16 ] , MABCQ [ 11 ] , MACQL [ 12 ] , and ICQ [ 4 ] extend single-agent methods to the multi-agent setting. For the diffusion policy, MADiff [ 7 ] models the joint policy as a diffusion process over the full action space, but we follow a distributed version ( MADiff-D ) that masks other agents’ information. DoF [ 8 ] factorizes the diffusion into per-agent components to satisfy decentralized execution. For the flow policy, Flow BC trains a per-agent flow-matching behavioral prior, and MAC-Flow [ 10 ] learns a joint flow and distills it into one-step projected policies with Q-maximization. sections.heading: 5.2 Experimental results
sections.text: RQ1 (Offline RL). Tables 1 and 2 report offline RL performance on SMACv1 and MA-MuJoCo. SCOUT achieves the highest average score on both benchmarks, outperforming all baselines across policy classes. The gain is consistent, i.e. , SCOUT matches or exceeds the best baseline on the majority of individual configurations. Notably, the advantage over MAC-Flow , which shares the same flow-matching backbone, isolates the benefit of test-time value transport over training-time distillation. Figure 3: Offline-to-online RL (8 seeds). Fine-tuning starts at normalized gradient steps 0.5 0.5 . RQ2 (Offline-to-online RL). Figure 3 evaluates how well each method transitions from offline pre-training to online fine-tuning. SCOUT outperforms MAC-Flow across all four scenarios. After the online transition, SCOUT continues to improve steadily. Because the behavioral prior is never deformed by a training-time value loss, it provides a stable foundation that online fine-tuning can build upon rather than correct. The advantage is most pronounced on Poor-quality datasets. Here, MAC-Flow ’s offline policy is anchored to low-quality demonstrations by its distillation objective, and online fine-tuning struggles to overcome this initialization. SCOUT , by contrast, treats the offline prior as a sampling distribution rather than a fixed policy, so the online phase simply adjusts the transport budget to exploit newly available data without inheriting the limitations of the offline dataset. Figure 4: Hyperparameter sweep. The plots show how different L L affect offline RL performance. RQ3 (Hyperparameter sensitivity). Figure 4 varies the refinement steps for training and test across four SMACv1-Medium scenarios. First, applying even a small number of refinement steps at test time improves over the no-refinement baseline ( L test = 0 L_{\text{test}}=0 ), confirming that decomposed value gradient transport adds meaningful coordination beyond best-of- P P selection alone. Second, the optimal L test L_{\text{test}} varies across scenarios. This is expected because each scenario and dataset quality presents a different Q-function landscape; the number of steps needed to reach high-value regions depends on how far the behavioral prior is from those regions and how smooth the Q-surface is. In practice, L test L_{\text{test}} can be selected via a small validation sweep at deployment time without retraining, which is precisely the adaptivity that training-time methods cannot offer.

sections.heading: 6 Conclusion
sections.text: In this paper, we propose SCOUT , the first test-time policy refinement framework for offline MARL that decouples behavioral modeling from value maximization. While prior generative policies often compromise expressiveness by integrating value guidance during training, SCOUT preserves the multi-modal behavioral prior and defers value-driven refinement strictly to test-time inference via decomposed Stein variational gradient transport. We provide a single-term KL bound on the joint soft-value gap under approximate IGM and constructively explain how additive TD targets transfer inter-agent dependencies into per-agent gradients. Limitation. While decoupling the behavioral prior from value maximization is effective across a range of tasks, the refinement hyperparameters exhibit some task- and dataset-dependent sensitivity. Therefore, a principled adaptive stopping criterion remains an open direction for future work.

sections.heading: B.1 Computational resources
sections.text: All experiments were conducted on a single server equipped with an Intel Xeon E5-2650 v3 CPU and an NVIDIA A40 GPU. The software stack consists of CUDA 12.2, cuDNN 8.9.7, Python 3.9, and JAX 0.4.30.

sections.heading: B.2 Implementation details
sections.text: Flow BC prior. We instantiate the foundation as a conditional flow-matching model that learns the behavior distribution of the offline dataset. Given an observation and a Gaussian noise sample, the actor parameterizes a velocity field that transports x 0 x_{0} to a data action x 1 x_{1} along the linear interpolation, trained by minimizing the flow-matching loss. At inference time, candidate actions are produced by a fixed-step Euler integration of the learned ODE, so the prior remains an explicit, multimodal generative model of the dataset rather than a unimodal collapse. Because the resulting samples are biased toward the modeled behavioral support, they encourage the agent to remain near in-distribution behaviors, while still preserving the diverse coordination patterns present in the offline corpus. Sinusoidal time embedding. The flow conditioning variable t ∈ [ 0 , 1 ] t\in[0,1] carries information about how close the current sample x t x_{t} is to data; feeding it as a raw scalar concatenated to the network input yields poor expressivity, since a single-channel signal interacts weakly with high-dimensional weights and forces the actor to learn very different behaviors at neighboring t t values from a one-dimensional cue. We therefore lift t t into a Fourier feature space φ ⁡ ( t ) = [ sin ⁡ ( 2 k ​ π ​ t ) , cos ⁡ ( 2 k ​ π ​ t ) ] k = 0 K − 1 ∈ ℝ 2 ​ K \varphi(t)=\bigl[\sin(2^{k}\pi t),\cos(2^{k}\pi t)\bigr]_{k=0}^{K-1}\in\mathbb{R}^{2K} with K = 8 K=8 , echoing the positional encodings widely used in diffusion and neural-field models. The exponentially spaced frequencies provide a multi-resolution decomposition of the time axis: low-frequency components encode the coarse phase of the integration trajectory while high-frequency components let the velocity field model sharp transitions near t = 0 t=0 and t = 1 t=1 . Online fine-tuning. After offline gradient steps, we roll out the policy and store the resulting trajectories in an online replay buffer. After an additional warm-up step with no online updates, each gradient step samples a 50 : 50 50:50 mixture of offline data and newly collected online data.

sections.heading: B.4 Baselines
sections.text: MADiff-D [ 7 ] . We utilize the official open-source implementation, specifically adopting the decentralized variant, MADiff-D , to align with our Dec-POMDP formulation. The model trains a conditional diffusion policy on centralized joint demonstrations but executes decentrally; each agent samples actions via reverse diffusion based solely on local observations while predicting teammates’ trajectories. We retain the original architecture and hyperparameters, applying a Gaussian DDPM scheduler with 200 200 denoising steps across all environments. DoF [ 8 ] . We use the official implementation of the DoF-Trajectory agent equipped with the W-concat factorization. All training and deployment configurations strictly follow the original paper. For action sampling, we similarly employ a Gaussian DDPM scheduler with 200 200 denoising steps for all environments. MAC-Flow [ 10 ] . We utilize the official open-source implementation. MAC-Flow models multi-modal data distributions via flow matching, utilizes a learned Q-function for guidance, and distills the guided flow into one-step decentralized policies. We maintain the original architecture and hyperparameters for all experiments.

sections.heading: Appendix C Additional Results
sections.text: Figure 5: Offline-to-online RL in MA-MuJoCo (8 seeds.) Offline-to-online RL. Figure 5 extends the offline-to-online evaluation to the continuous control domain. Across all six configurations, SCOUT demonstrates consistent improvement after the online transition at normalized step 0.5 0.5 . These empirical results suggest that the undeformed flow prior allows the transport budget to flexibly exploit newly collected interaction data. Together with the SMACv1 results in Figure 3 , SCOUT achieves positive online improvement in all offline-to-online RL configurations across both benchmarks, confirming that the test-time transport paradigm generalizes across discrete and continuous action space types. Figure 6: Hyperparameter sweep on MA-MuJoCo. Hyperparameter sweep. Figure 6 reports the sensitivity of SCOUT to the refinement steps L train L_{\text{train}} and L test L_{\text{test}} across all four dataset qualities in MA-MuJoCo. In the Expert and Medium-Expert datasets, performance is largely insensitive to the choice of L test L_{\text{test}} , which is expected because the behavioral prior already closely matches high-value regions, leaving little room for gradient transport to improve upon. In contrast, the Medium and Medium-Replay datasets exhibit a clearer benefit from moderate refinement steps, where increasing L test L_{\text{test}} from 0 to 3 yields substantial gains. However, excessive refinement L test = 10 L_{\text{test}}=10 can degrade performance in some cases, suggesting that the critic’s accuracy degrades when actions are transported too far from the behavioral support.

Learn more × Back to arXiv License: CC BY 4.0 arXiv:2610.02554v1 [cs.LG] 01 Oct 2026 Test-time Multi-agent Coordination by Decomposed Value Gradient Flow Dongsu Lee Haoran Xu Amy Zhang Affiliation: The University of Texas at Austin Email: dongsu.lee@utexas.edu Affiliation: https://github.com/DongsuLeeTech/scout.git Abstract Offline multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) faces a persistent trade-off. Expressive generative policies can represent multi-modal coordination in the data, but cannot distinguish high-value regions, while value-optimized policies exploit the learned Q-function but collapse the multi-modal into a single dominant mode. A single agent’s mode collapse can break joint coordination, and simultaneous drift across agents can push the joint policy into unseen regions of the action space. We propose scalable coordination via optimal unified transport (SCOUT) , the first offline MARL framework to combine a generative foundation model with a learned value function through test-time action refinement. SCOUT trains two decoupled components: a flow-matching behavioral prior and a decomposed value function. At test-time, it transports behavioral samples toward high-value regions via Stein variational gradient descent. The number of transport steps controls adaptive test-time scaling, replacing a fixed regularization coefficient. Under the individual-global-max (IGM) principle, we prove a single-term KL bound on the joint soft-value gap that vanishes as transport converges, with an irreducible additive residual proportional to the IGM violation. Empirically, SCOUT achieves the best average performance across discrete and continuous offline MARL benchmarks and yields performance improvements in all offline-to-online configurations. Figure 1: Overview of the proposed solution. ( a ) The prerequisite for SCOUT is to train the reference policy via flow matching and decomposed value via a value decomposition network (VDN). ( b ) SCOUT transports the behavior distribution at test time via Stein variational gradient descent. 1 Introduction Offline MARL is motivated by the need to learn coordinated multi-agent behaviors in safety-critical or cost-constrained domains where active data collection is infeasible or expensive, e.g. , autonomous driving [ 1 ] , logistics [ 2 ] , and robotics [ 3 ] . In this setting, the learning objective is twofold. Agents must learn to coordinate their behavior from heterogeneous and suboptimal demonstrations, while avoiding the distributional shift that arises when the learned policy visits state-action regions unsupported by the data. Early offline MARL methods [ 4 , 5 , 6 ] rely on simple policy classes ( i.e. , Gaussian), which struggle to represent multi-modal and coordinated joint action distributions. When offline data contains a mixture of diverse coordination strategies, a unimodal policy often collapses onto a single mode and produces out-of-distribution joint actions that no agent in the data ever executed together. To address this expressiveness gap, recent works adopt powerful generative models, including diffusion models [ 7 , 8 ] and flow matching models [ 9 , 10 ] , as policy representations in offline MARL. Although these models improve the representational power of policy, their iterative sampling process incurs a high inference cost. MAC-Flow [ 10 ] and OM 2 P [ 9 ] mitigate this via one-step distillation and mean-flow generation, respectively. However, improved expressiveness and faster inference do not resolve a more fundamental limitation. Since the outcome policy is optimized against a learned Q-function, it inherently tends to collapse diverse coordination modes into a single or blurred one. Methods that parameterize a policy and optimize it to maximize a learned Q-function must balance value improvement against staying close to the behavioral distribution. A fixed regularization coefficient controls this trade-off. If it is too large, the policy stays too close to suboptimal data; if it is too small, the policy exploits errors in the learned Q-function and produces OOD actions. Although this tension is well-known in single-agent offline RL [ 11 , 12 ] , the multi-agent setting introduces the following compounding difficulty. Training-time value maximization deforms each agent’s policy away from the behavioral prior, and the regularization coefficient bounds how far each marginal may drift, but cannot bound the compound effect on the joint. Even when every marginal remains within its individual support, the joint policy can place mass on action combinations that no trajectory in the data ever visited ( i.e. , regions where the learned Q-function is least reliable). In fact, the data may support multiple distinct joint modes of comparably high estimated value, but committing each marginal to a single greedy mode at training time discards the others before the agent has any way to tell them apart. Once new interaction data arrives, the policy can no longer use it to discriminate which mode is truly higher-value, because the alternatives have already been suppressed. A natural alternative is to decouple two objectives, motivated by test-time training [ 13 , 14 , 15 ] . Instead of learning a policy that directly maximizes value, we keep the behavioral policy as a foundational prior and defer value-based refinement to test time. At deployment, we sample action candidates from this prior and then move them toward high-value regions using value gradients. The extent of this adjustment acts as adaptive control, replacing the need for a fixed regularization coefficient. In this work, we ask a question not yet studied by prior works: How do we avoid explicit policy parameterization for value maximization, and instead recover coordination at test time by directly transporting behavioral samples toward high-value regions? We answer this question with the proposed solution, SCOUT (scalable coordination via optimal unified transport) , an offline MARL framework that combines flow-matching behavioral priors with decomposed value gradient for test-time action refinement. Our key contributions are: • We propose a policy-free value maximization for offline MARL that separates behavioral modeling from value improvement, replacing training-time regularization tuning with a test-time refinement budget. • We derive decomposed value gradient transport under the IGM principle, enabling fully decentralized test-time refinement that recovers inter-agent coordination with a bounded approximation gap. • Empirically, test-time refinement strengthens coordination without retraining, achieving the best average performance in continuous and discrete domains. Notably, unlike existing flow-based MARL, our method yields improvements in all offline-to-online RL experiments. 2 Related Works Offline MARL. Several works have explored the data-driven sequential decision-making problem, including offline RL and MARL, which aims to extract a return-maximizing policy within the support of an offline dataset. Specifically, offline MARL requires learning coordinated policies for multiple agents. This is not trivial because it requires modeling dependencies among agents in a combinatorially large joint action space. The simplest baselines are multi-agent extensions of single-agent offline RL methods, either by introducing conservatism in the value function [ 11 , 12 ] or the actor [ 16 ] , or by performing Bellman updates without querying out-of-distribution actions [ 17 ] . To further promote coordination, more advanced works are often combined with additional multi-agent design choices, such as value decomposition [ 5 , 18 ] , policy optimization with a centralized critic [ 4 , 6 ] , or a centralized world model [ 19 ] . However, these methods often struggle to capture the multi-modal distributions present in multi-agent offline datasets because of their limited policy expressiveness. To address this issue, recent work has adopted more expressive generative policies, including an autoregressive model [ 20 ] , diffusion models [ 7 ] , and flow matching [ 10 ] . However, these methods couple value learning with the generative process itself: they either anchor the policy via BC-like losses [ 21 , 22 , 10 , 23 ] , which produces overly conservative behavior, or backpropagate value gradients through iterative sampling [ 24 , 25 ] , which is unstable. In contrast, the proposed solution bypasses explicit policy parameterization altogether. Instead, Stein variational gradient [ 26 , 27 , 14 ] fields refine flow-generated action candidates toward high-value regions at test time. This enables adaptive test-time scaling while retaining generative expressiveness. Test-time action refinement. Our main idea in this work is based on test-time refinement ( i.e. , a ← a + ∇ a Q ​ ( s , a ) a\leftarrow a+\nabla_{a}Q(s,a) ) [ 13 ] , which refines actions from a base generative policy at inference time rather than during training. This paradigm has been explored along several directions in single-agent RL. Rejection sampling methods generate multiple action candidates and select the highest-valued one [ 28 , 29 ] . Gradient-based approaches directly optimize sampled actions via Q-function gradients [ 25 , 14 , 30 ] . Residual policies instead train a separate network to modify a base policy in noise or action space [ 31 , 32 ] . Complementary to these, optimal transport (OT) offers a principled framework for moving probability mass toward high-value regions [ 33 , 34 ] . More recently, particle-based methods adopt an OT viewpoint to transport samples toward value-preferred regions [ 35 ] . However, these approaches remain limited to single-agent settings. The proposed solution is motivated by this direction but specifically designed to solve the multi-agent coordination problem. This avoids explicit policy parameterization and naturally handles the combinatorial joint action space. 3 Preliminaries Problem setting. Why do we need an implicit policy? This direction offers several appealing properties. First, because the initial actions are drawn from the behavioral policy, the implicit policy refines the behavioral prior rather than replacing it. Then, the transport budget provides an adaptive test-time scaling. When L = 0 L=0 , it recovers the best sampling from the behavioral policy, while increasing L L progressively pushes actions toward Q-maximizing regions. Furthermore, the gradient-based transport can discover actions beyond the reference distribution when the Q-function generalizes well. 4.1 Why is this hard in multi-agent settings? The above idea and problem hold straightforwardly in the single-agent setting [ 14 , 48 ] , where the transport operates on a single action space 𝒜 \mathcal{A} guided by a single Q-function. However, extending this to multi-agent settings is non-trivial. Under the CTDE paradigm, each agent i i can only access its local observation o i o_{i} at test time. This means the action refinement must run independently for each agent, using only its local Q-function Q i ​ ( o i , a i ) Q_{i}(o_{i},a_{i}) and its own action particles. The refined joint action ( a 1 ∗ , … , a I ∗ ) (a_{1}^{*},\ldots,a_{I}^{*}) must be globally coherent. Namely, each agent’s refined action should be coordinated with those of other agents. This tension between decentralized execution and coordinated behavior has been a long-standing challenge in MARL [ 39 , 40 ] . The most common solution is the IGM principle [ 39 ] in ( 1 ), which ensures independent per-agent maximization to align with joint maximization. However, several practical questions remain. First, IGM guarantees alignment at the greedy argmax, but the gradient-based transport involves iterative updates that modify the particle distribution across multiple steps. It is unclear whether the per-agent transport dynamics remain aligned with the joint optimum throughout this process, especially when the critic must evaluate actions that are progressively shifted away from the behavioral support during training. Second, the individual behavioral prior might discard the inter-agent correlations present in the offline data. Even if the transport dynamics are correctly factorized, the initial particles may lack the coordination patterns necessary for effective joint behavior. 4.2 Proposed solution In this subsection, we now present the full SCOUT framework for multi-agent test-time coordination.
